'''Robert Harry Socolow''' (born December 27, 1937; surname pronunciation sŏc'-ŏ-lō) is an American [[Environmental science|environmental scientist]], [[theoretical physicist]] and professor emeritus of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering at [[Princeton University]]. He was a founder of the Carbon Mitigation Initiative of Princeton University. He has articulated pathways to reduction of carbon dioxide emissions for minimizing climate change, especially the concept of [[climate stabilization wedge]]. Socolow has developed equitable approaches to [[climate change mitigation]] that balance reductions in greenhouse gas emissions with economic development.<ref name="ShortBio">{{cite web |title=Robert H. Socolow |url=https://mae.princeton.edu/people/faculty/socolow |website=mae.princeton.edu |publisher=Princeton University |access-date=24 March 2024}}</ref><ref name="ScottMedal" />

Socolow was a 2023 recipient of the [[John Scott Medal]] for his innovations in environmental science and climate stabilization. The award citation highlighted his ability to frame environmental problems in practical terms that aid in consensus-building.<ref name="ScottMedal">{{cite web |title=The John Scott Award |url=https://thejohnscottaward.github.io/jsc/recent.html |website=thejohnscottaward.github.io |publisher=Board of Directors of City Trusts of Philadelphia |access-date=10 March 2024}}</ref>

The [[American Physical Society]] stated that Socolow had a leadership role in establishing energy and environmental problems as interdisciplinary research fields for physicists consistent with the highest scientific standards.<ref name="SzilardAward">{{cite web |title=2003 Leo Szilard Lectureship Award Recipient |url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Socolow&first_nm=Robert&year=2003 |website=aps.org |publisher=American Physical Society |access-date=10 March 2024}}</ref> In this regard, with ecologist [[John Harte (scientist)|John Harte]], in 1971 Socolow authored ''Patient Earth'' which was an early casebook on environmental science.<ref name="BookReview">{{cite journal |last1=Gollub |first1=Jerry P. |title=Book Reviews: Patient Earth |journal=American Journal of Physics |date=May 1, 1972 |page=786 |doi=10.1119/1.1986663 |url=https://pubs.aip.org/aapt/ajp/article-abstract/40/5/786/1049237/Patient-Earth?redirectedFrom=fulltext |access-date=12 March 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref> His research was characterized as pioneering in energy efficiency research in the context of environmentalism. Socolow's scientific investigations influenced the decision to cancel the Miami Jetport project and the Tocks Island Dam project in northern New Jersey. He articulated approaches to industrialization of the [[Developing country|developing countries]] through environmentally responsible means.<ref name="Davidson">Davidson, Martha. "Portrait of Innovation: Robert H. Socolow." ''Inventing for the Environment'', Arthur Molella and Joyce Bedi (eds), The MIT Press (publisher), 2003, pp. 373–382, ISBN 0-262-13427-6.</ref>

==Early life and education==
Socolow was born in 1937 in New York City to parents Abraham Walter Socolow and Edith Socolow (née Gutman). He attended the [[Ethical Culture Fieldston School]]. His father, A. Walter Socolow, was a founder of the [[Reconstructionist Rabbinical College]] of Pennsylvania and served as president of the Board of Jewish Education of Greater New York and also the [[Society for the Advancement of Judaism]].<ref name="Marriage">{{cite news |title=Miss Sussman, Vassar Alumna, Becomes Bride; Wears Peau de Soie at Marriage in Suburb to Robert Socolow |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1962/06/11/archives/miss-sussman-vassar-alumna-becomes-bride-wears-peau-de-soie-at.html |access-date=10 February 2024 |agency=The New York Times |date=June 11, 1962}}</ref><ref name="WalterObit">{{cite news |title=A. Walter Socolow, Jewish Reconstructionist, 87 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/12/17/obituaries/a-walter-socolow-jewish-reconstructionist-87.html |access-date=14 March 2024 |agency=The New York Times |date=December 17, 1994}}</ref>

Socolow graduated summa cum laude in 1959 from Harvard College with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in physics. Through a program at Harvard, he traveled for a year in Africa and Asia, having been awarded a Frederick Sheldon Travel Scholarship. Socolow then earned his Ph.D. in physics from Harvard University working on theoretical problems, finishing his doctorate in 1964. His doctoral thesis was on "Electromagnetic Self-Energies and Weak Decays in Unitary Symmetry" which was research conducted with Harvard professor [[Sidney Coleman]].<ref name=princeton>{{cite web|url= http://www.princeton.edu/mae/people/faculty/socolow/|title=Biography|publisher=Princeton University|access-date=June 17, 2013}}</ref> Between 1964 and 1966 he was [[National Science Foundation]] Postdoctoral Fellow in Physics, at the [[University of California, Berkeley|University of California at Berkeley]] and the [[European Center for Nuclear Research]] (CERN) in [[Geneva|Geneva, Switzerland]].<ref name="Davidson" />

In 1962 Socolow married literary scholar [[Elizabeth Socolow]] (née Sussman).<ref name="Marriage">{{cite news |title=Miss Sussman, Vassar Alumna, Becomes Bride; Wears Peau de Soie at Marriage in Suburb to Robert Socolow |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1962/06/11/archives/miss-sussman-vassar-alumna-becomes-bride-wears-peau-de-soie-at.html |access-date=10 February 2024 |agency=The New York Times |date=June 11, 1962}}</ref>

Socolow's upbringing and early education emphasized arts, culture, and languages. He became multilingual, especially French and Russian.<ref name="Davidson" /> Socolow has stated his parents and teachers instilled in him with a sense of ''[[Weltschmerz]]'' (melancholy about the state of the world) and [[Tikkun olam|''Tikkun Olam'']] (relating to actions for the restoration of the world).<ref>Robert Socolow [https://socolow.princeton.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/375/2016/01/Georgetown-Weiss-appreciation.3.28.14.pdf The road ahead for planetary environmentalism: An appreciation of Charles Weiss] Workshop: "An engaged life of science in the interest of humanity
" Chuckfest, Georgetown University. March 28, 2014</ref>

In 1957 during his undergraduate years, Socolow worked as a summer student at the [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]]. His time there exposed him to the rapid advances in the field of particle physics and convinced him to pursue an undergraduate degree in physics. Later, in 1961 when Socolow was in graduate school, he worked at the [[Pugwash Conferences on Science and World Affairs]] at which time he realized that scientific rigor is useful in developing public policy.<ref name="Davidson" />

==Career==
In 1966, Socolow joined the faculty at [[Yale University]] as an assistant professor of physics, where he remained until 1971. During the period shortly after completing his doctorate, Socolow continued his research in theoretical physics, collaborating with physicist [[Sheldon Glashow]]. They published jointly on aspects of [[Meson|mesons]] and other [[Subatomic particle|subatomic particles]].<ref name="Glashow">{{cite journal |last1=Glashow |first1=Sheldon L. |last2=Socolow |first2=Robert H. |title=Decay Modes of Spin-Two Mesons |journal=Physical Review Letters |date=16 August 1965 |volume=15 |issue=7 |pages=329–333 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.329 |bibcode=1965PhRvL..15..329G |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.15.329 |access-date=10 March 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

While at Yale, Socolow and other faculty members organized a "Day of Reflection" to discuss the role of scientists in the military and the [[Vietnam War]], as part of the [[peace movement]] of the era. The event was held on March 4, 1969.<ref name="AntiWar">{{cite web |last1=Nova |first1=Max |title=The Bet: Paul Ehrlich, Julian Simon, and Our Gamble over Earth's Future |url=https://books.max-nova.com/the-bet/ |website=books.max-nova.com |date=21 August 2017 |publisher=Book Reviews |access-date=21 March 2024}}</ref>

===Environmental research===
In 1969, through his antiwar activities, Socolow became acquainted with then Princeton physics professor [[Marvin Leonard Goldberger|Marvin Goldberger]]. Goldberger encouraged Socolow to participate in a summer case study program sponsored by the [[National Academy of Sciences]] at [[Stanford University]] on management of the environment. With fellow participant and Yale colleague John Harte, Socolow evaluated the environmental impact of the proposed [[Dade-Collier Training and Transition Airport|Big Cypress Jetport]] in the [[Everglades|Florida Everglades]]. They concluded that the impact on local water supplies was too large to justify continued construction of the airport. This study was influential in the decision to discontinue the project. As a result of this experience, Socolow redirected his scientific investigations and career endeavors to matters related to environmentalism, energy efficiency and sustainable development.<ref name="Davidson" />

Shortly thereafter, Socolow and Harte published ''Patient Earth'', which was an early casebook on environmental science.<ref name="Davidson" />

Partly through the influence of Marvin Goldberger, in 1971 Socolow moved to Princeton University, with the rank of Associate Professor, serving in the Department of Aerospace and Mechanical Sciences, with the responsibility of organizing its newly created Center for Environmental Studies. An early endeavor at Princeton was the Twin Rivers Project, in which Socolow led a study that included several members of the Princeton faculty to evaluate the energy efficiency of individual homes at the [[Twin Rivers, New Jersey|Twin Rivers]] housing development in New Jersey. Twin Rivers was a middle class housing development in [[Mercer County, New Jersey|Mercer County]]. The study lasted seven years and evaluated energy usage in ordinary middle class homes and ways of improving the energy efficiency of individual homes. The project outcome was reported in a book ''Saving Energy in the Home: Princeton's Experiments at Twin Rivers'', in which they showed that a 75% reduction in energy consumption was possible.<ref name="Davidson" />

Beginning in 1972, Socolow led a study of the environmental impact of the [[Tocks Island Dam controversy|Tocks Island Dam]] project, which was the proposed construction of a dam in the [[Delaware Water Gap]] between Pennsylvania and New Jersey. This was to be the largest dam constructed in the eastern portion of the United States. Socolow assembled a multi-disciplinary team to conduct the evaluation, and his team issued a report entitled ''Boundaries of Analysis: An Inquiry into the Tocks Island Dam Controversy''. Ultimately political decision makers canceled the project.<ref name="Davidson" />

A [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] and [[German Marshall Fund]] Fellowship from 1976 to 1977 enabled Socolow to study international energy issues at [[Cavendish Laboratory]], University of Cambridge, U.K. In 1977 he became full professor and Associate Director of Princeton's Center for Energy and Environmental Studies. Socolow was also a faculty member in the [[Princeton University School of Engineering and Applied Science]]. During this time period, Socolow also taught frequently in the Woodrow Wilson School of Public and International Affairs.<ref name="Davidson" /><ref name="BestArticles" />

Socolow continued at Princeton University, serving as director of the university's Center for Energy and Environment Studies from 1979 to 1997.<ref name="IAP">{{cite web |title=Robert Socolow |url=https://www.interacademies.org/person/robert-socolow |website=interacademies.org |publisher=The Interacademy Partnership |access-date=11 March 2024}}</ref> During his tenure at the CEES, Socolow worked on initiatives that would enable economic advancements of the developing world that are environmentally responsible, approaches to environmentally improved means of delivering nitrogen fertilizer in agricultural settings, economically viable approaches to [[carbon sequestration]] for reduction of atmospheric carbon dioxide levels, and [[industrial ecology]]. He further contended that each generation has a moral and ethical obligation to leave successive generations with improved means for [[environmental stewardship]].<ref name="Davidson" />

Socolow worked with physicist [[Frank N. von Hippel]] and others on approaches to electricity generation through nuclear fission while rendering inaccessible the plutonium isotopes that could be used for fabrication of weapons. Socolow advocated nuclear power constrained in this way as an environmentally benign approach to electricity generation.<ref name="VonHippel">{{cite journal | doi=10.1080/25751654.2019.1698504 | title=Citizen Scientist: Frank von Hippel's Adventures in Nuclear Arms Control | date=2020 | last1=von Hippel | first1=Frank | last2=Kurokawa | first2=Tomoko | journal=Journal for Peace and Nuclear Disarmament | volume=3 | pages=38–68 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

Princeton University president [[Robert F. Goheen]] had significant interest in matters related to energy and the environment, and he believed that Princeton could have a leadership role in such matters. To this end, he recruited Socolow to Princeton University, charging him with developing a multidisciplinary approach to energy and the environment. In 1971, Socolow moved to Princeton's newly-formed CEES and became a faculty member of the university's School of Engineering and Applied Science.<ref name="CMIhistory">{{cite web |last1=Seltzer |first1=Molly A. |title=Princeton: A Half-Century at the Environmental Forefront |url=https://acee.princeton.edu/acee-news/history-50-years-of-energy-research/ |website=acee.princeton.edu |date=21 August 2020 |publisher=Princeton University |access-date=25 March 2024}}</ref>

===Carbon mitigation initiative===

Beginning in 2000, Socolow collaborated with Princeton colleagues [[Robert H. Williams (physicist)|Robert H. Williams]] and [[Stephen W. Pacala]] to establish the carbon mitigation initiative (CMI). The goal of CMI was to address the problem of anthropogenic climate change through more effective management and reduction of atmospheric carbon dioxide emissions. CMI was established as a long term project, funded as of 2024 through 2025. The initiative was sponsored by [[BP]] with some initial participation by the [[Ford Motor Company]].<ref name="CMIhistory" />

Through their collaboration at CMI, Socolow and Pacala conceived of the idea of climate stabilization wedges. The intent was to devise manageable and realistic approaches to stabilize carbon dioxide emissions to the atmosphere at current levels for a duration of 50 years. The "stabilization triangle" is the area in the graph of carbon dioxide emissions versus time between projected future atmospheric emissions of carbon dioxide compared to constant emissions at current levels. Socolow and Pacal divided the stabilization triangle into triangular "wedges," each of which describes a specific amount of carbon dioxide emissions mitigation based on the application of a particular currently existing technology.<ref name="SciAm">{{cite journal |last1=Socolow |first1=Robert H. |last2=Pacala |first2=Stephen W. |title=A Plan to Keep Carbon in Check |journal=Scientific American |date=September 2006 |volume=295 |issue=3 |pages=50–57 |doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0906-50 |pmid=16925035 |bibcode=2006SciAm.295c..50S |url=https://www1.udel.edu/igert/pbl_course/Socolow%20and%20Pacala%20Problem.pdf |access-date=25 March 2024}}</ref><ref name="SciAmLashof">{{cite journal |last1=Lashof |first1=Daniel A. |title=U.S. Stabilization Wedges |journal=Scientific American |date=July 27, 2006 |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/us-stabilization-wedges/ |access-date=25 March 2024}}</ref>

As first published, the climate stabilization wedges consisted of seven wedges which in combination would provide the needed carbon dioxide mitigation. These could be selected from existing technologies that include: Energy efficiency and conservation; Improved power generation; Carbon sequestration; Alternative energy sources; and Agriculture / Forestry. The wedges selected need not be the same for the [[Developing country|Developing world]] and the [[Developed country|Industrialized world]]. Socolow and Pacala first published the concept of climate stabilization wedges in the journal ''Science'' in 2004.<ref name="SciAm" /><ref name="Science">{{Cite journal |last1=Pacala |first1=S. |last2=Socolow |first2=R. |author2-link=Robert H. Socolow |date=2004-08-13 |title=Stabilization Wedges: Solving the Climate Problem for the Next 50 Years with Current Technologies |journal=Science |language=en |volume=305 |issue=5686 |pages=968–972 |bibcode=2004Sci...305..968P |doi=10.1126/science.1100103 |issn=0036-8075 |pmid=15310891 |s2cid=2203046}}</ref>

Emphasizing the implementation of existing technologies as a portfolio of options for carbon dioxide mitigation, Socolow and Pacala stated in the journal ''Scientific American'':
<blockquote>
"Holding carbon dioxide emissions constant for 50 years, without choking off economic growth, is within our grasp."<ref name="SciAm" />
</blockquote>

The book ''An Inconvenient Truth'' by former United States Vice President [[Al Gore]] referred to Socolow and Pacala{{efn|''An Inconvenient Truth'' refers to Socolow and Pacala as economists rather than environmental scientists.}} and their work on climate stabilization wedges, emphasizing that the needed technology is already available to halt rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide levels.<ref name="Gore">{{cite book |last1=Gore |first1=Al |title=An Inconvenient Truth: The Planetary Emergency of Global Warming and What We Can Do About It |date=2006 |publisher=Rodale |location=New York |isbn=978-1-59486-567-1 |pages=280–281}}</ref>

===Later career===
In a 2009 scientific publication with ecologist [[G. David Tilman]] and others, Socolow cautioned against [[Biofuel|biofuels]] that are implemented poorly. Tilman and Socolow's scientific publication on the subject stated that biofuels should not compete with food crops or cause land-clearing and that they should offer overall greenhouse gas emissions as indicated by [[life cycle analysis]].<ref name="ScienceTilman">{{cite journal |last1=Tilman |first1=G. David |last2=Socolow |first2=Robert H. |last3=Foley |first3=Jonathan A. |last4=Hill |first4=Jason |last5=Larson |first5=Eric |last6=Lynd |first6=Lee |last7=Pacala |first7=Stephen |last8=Reilly |first8=John |last9=Searchinger |first9=Tim |last10=Williams |first10=Robert |last11=Somerville |first11=Chris |title=Beneficial Biofuels—The Food, Energy, and Environment Trilemma |journal=Science |date=17 July 2009 |volume=325 |issue=5938 |pages=270–271 |doi=10.1126/science.1177970 |pmid=19608900 |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1177970 |access-date=8 April 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Biofuels">{{cite journal |last1=Rist |first1=Lucy |last2=Lee |first2=Janice Ser Huay |last3=Koh |first3=Lian Pin |title=Biofuels: Social Benefits |journal=Science |date=4 December 2009 |volume=326 |issue=5958 |page=1346 |doi=10.1126/science.326.5958.1346-b |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.326.5958.1346-b |access-date=8 April 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In his on-going involvement with Princeton's Andinger Center for Energy and the Environment, Socolow led a group that wrote a series of environmentally-relevant [[Monograph|monographs]] covering such topics as wind and solar power, grid power storage, small scale nuclear reactors, and [[nuclear fusion]].<ref name="ShortBio" />

Socolow coined the term "destiny studies" in 2012 as a planetary-wide, interdisciplinary view of what Earth could look like.{{efn|At times Socolow used the term destiny science, instead of destiny studies, emphasizing the role of scientists in visualizing long term environmental effects of human activity.<ref name="Bulletin">{{cite web |last1=Socolow |first1=Robert |title=Destiny Science for the Anthropocene |url=https://thebulletin.org/2024/01/destiny-science-for-the-anthropocene/ |website=thebulletin.org |date=19 January 2024 |publisher=Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists |access-date=8 April 2024}}</ref>}} Following his 2013 retirement from his professorship, Socolow became an [[Emeritus|emeritus professor]], while continuing his research at Princeton University. Destiny studies became an on-going endeavor at Princeton University and was the subject of a 2019 symposium conducted in honor of Socolow's retirement from full professorship.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.engineeringchallenges.org/cms/7124/7274.aspx|title=Robert Socolow|publisher=[[National Academy of Engineering]]|date= n.d.|access-date=3 November 2017}}</ref><ref name="Forbes">{{cite news |last1=del Castillo |first1=Michael |title=Unwinding Doomsday's Clock |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/michaeldelcastillo/2021/12/26/unwinding-doomsdays-clock/?sh=113c1cae5558 |access-date=1 April 2024 |agency=Forbes |date=December 26, 2021}}</ref><ref name="DestinySymposium">{{cite web |title=Destiny Studies for a Small Planet |url=https://environment.princeton.edu/destiny-studies/ |website=environment.princeton.edu |publisher=Princeton University |access-date=1 April 2024}}</ref>

Around the same time, Socolow articulated practical approaches to climate change mitigation based on an analysis of demand, supply and the relationship to international politics, as well as the role of populations growth. He acknowledged the uncertainty in the degree of urgency and that resistance is natural and to be expected. He discussed impediments resulting from factions that rarely communicate with one another, such as the [[Nuclear power|nuclear power industry]] and the [[renewable fuels|renewable fuels industry]].<ref name="Vandy">Robert H. Socolow, "[https://scholarship.law.vanderbilt.edu/vlr/vol65/iss6/2/ Truths We Must Tell Ourselves to Manage Climate Change]", 65 Vanderbilt Law Review 1455 (2019).</ref>

Regarding the impact of the developing world on climate change, Socolow stated that an equitable approach is through the concept of the personal carbon footprint, which emphasized emissions of carbon dioxide through activities of individuals rather than societies as a whole. The basis of this method of analysis is that affluent people in the developing world account for the majority of the carbon dioxide emissions within nations of the developing world even though they are a small portion of the population. Socolow first articulated the concept of the personal carbon footprint in a 2006 journal article of the ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]'' co-authored by his colleague Pacala.<ref name="Vandy" /><ref name="IndividualEmissions">{{cite web |last1=McPherson |first1=Kitta |title=New Princeton Method may help Allocate Carbon Emissions Responsibility Among Nations |url=https://www.princeton.edu/news/2009/07/06/new-princeton-method-may-help-allocate-carbon-emissions-responsibility-among |website=princeton.edu |publisher=Princeton University |access-date=4 April 2024}}</ref>

In a follow-up publication, Socolow and his co-authors elaborated on the responsibilities of "high emitters" who reside in developing nations.<ref name="PNAS">{{cite journal | doi=10.1073/pnas.0905232106 | title=Sharing global CO <sub>2</sub> emission reductions among one billion high emitters | date=2009 | last1=Chakravarty | first1=Shoibal | last2=Chikkatur | first2=Ananth | last3=De Coninck | first3=Heleen | last4=Pacala | first4=Stephen | last5=Socolow | first5=Robert | last6=Tavoni | first6=Massimo | journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | volume=106 | issue=29 | pages=11884–11888 | doi-access=free | pmid=19581586 | pmc=2706272 | bibcode=2009PNAS..10611884C }}</ref>

Socolow pointed out the environmental impact of population growth and its role in [[population ecology]].<ref name="Vandy" />

In a scientific publication that refers to "witnessing for the middle", Socolow advocated for a middle ground that avoids overstating the case for drastic environmental actions while simultaneously preserving a sense of urgency among the public and policy makers. He contended that this middle ground minimizes polarization of climate change issues.<ref name="Daedalus">{{cite journal |last1=Rosenblum |first1=Nancy L. |title=Introduction: Paths to Witnessing, Ethics of Speaking out |journal=Daedalus |date=2020 |volume=149 |issue=4 |pages=6–24 |doi=10.1162/daed_e_01813 |url=https://direct.mit.edu/daed/article/149/4/6/94872/Introduction-Paths-to-Witnessing-Ethics-of |access-date=8 April 2024|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

With colleague Chris Grieg, Socolow published an opinion piece in [[The Washington Post]] stating that there can be an important role for the fossil fuel industry while simultaneously reducing carbon dioxide emissions through [[carbon sequestration]].<ref name="WaPo2023">{{cite news |last1=Socolow |first1=Robert H. |last2=Greig |first2=Chris |title=Opinion: Hate Fossil Fuels? Give Them a Role and get to Clean Energy Quicker |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2023/11/13/carbon-capture-cop28-compromise/ |access-date=8 March 2024 |agency=The Washington Post |date=November 13, 2023}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Socolow resides in Princeton, New Jersey, with his partner, Mimi Schwartz, a writer and scholar of creative non-fiction. He has two sons and was married three times. Elizabeth Anne (Sussman) Socolow is a published poet. The late Dr. Jane Reis Pitt, a physician-scientist, was a researcher on HIV pediatric infections at Columbia Presbyterian. Emily Matthews is an editor who worked for many years at the [[World Resources Institute]].<ref name="Davidson" />

Socolow and his siblings established the annual A. Walter Socolow Writing Prize to honor their deceased father.<ref name="WritingPrize">{{cite web |title=The A. Walter Socolow Writing Prize |url=https://www.rrc.edu/files/rrc_2022_graduationprogram_web.pdf |website=rrc.edu |publisher=Reconstructionist Rabbinical College |access-date=14 March 2024}}</ref>

==Awards and recognition==
From 1992 to 2002 Socolow was an editor for ''[[Annual Review of Energy and the Environment]].'' He served on two committees of the [[United States National Academies|National Academies]]: America's Energy Future and America's Climate Choices and in 2004 became lifetime national associate of the National Academy of Sciences. He received the [[Leo Szilard Lectureship Award]] in 2003. The Szilard Lectureship Award citation stated about Socolow, "for leadership in establishing energy and environmental problems as legitimate research fields for physicists, and for demonstrating that these broadly defined problems can be addressed with the highest scientific standards".<ref name=princeton/>

Socolow is a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (elected in 1983)<ref>{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=1983&unit_id=&institution=Princeton+University}}</ref> and of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].<ref name="princeton" />

[[Time (magazine)]] in 2007 recognized Socolow and Pacala's concept of climate stabilization wedges as a means of addressing some of Earth's most difficult problems.<ref name="Time2007">{{cite journal |last1=Lemonick |first1=Michael D. |title=Robert Socolow and Stephen Pacala |journal=Time Magazine |date=April 2, 2007}}</ref> Then, in 2009, Time listed the "personal carbon footprint" as number 12 on the list of 50 best inventions of the year. Socolow and other Princeton colleagues were inventors on the personal carbon footprint concept.<ref name="Time2009">{{cite journal |title=The 50 Best Inventions of 2009 |journal=Time Magazine |date=December 8, 2009}}</ref>

Socolow and Pacala's publication in the journal ''Scientific American'', "A Plan to Keep Carbon in Check", was one of 28 scientific articles included in the 2007 edition of the book ''The Best American Science and Nature Writing''.<ref name="BestArticles">{{cite book |last1=Preston |first1=Richard |title=The Best American Science and Nature Writing |date=2007 |publisher=Houghton Mifflin |location=Boston |isbn=978-0-618-72224-2 |pages=259–267}}</ref>

In 2010, Socolow received the Keystone Award for Leadership in the Environment from the Keystone Center of Colorado.<ref name="Keystone">{{cite web |last1=Ricci |first1=Dana |title=Socolow Honored for Environmental Achievement |url=https://environment.princeton.edu/news/socolow-honored-for-environmental-achievement/ |website=environment.princeton.edu |publisher=High Meadows Environmental Institute |access-date=2 March 2024}}</ref> He was a 2023 winner of the [[John Scott Medal]] for his career-long contributions for understanding and addressing anthropogenic climate change.<ref name="ScottMedal" />

Socolow served on the [[Deutsche Bank]] Climate Change Advisory Board from 2008 to 2017 and on the [[United States Department of Energy|U.S. Department of Energy]] Task Force on Carbon Dioxide Utilization.<ref name="DB">{{cite web |last1=Miltner |first1=Sabine |last2=Dieckmann |first2=Julia |title=Sustainability at Deutsche Bank |url=https://investor-relations.db.com/files/documents/other-presentations-and-events/JD_SRI__Roadshow_New_York_Boston_25_27_June_2012_final.pdf?language_id=1 |website=investor-relations.db.com |publisher=Deutsche Bank |access-date=8 April 2024}}</ref><ref name="DeptEnergy">{{cite web |title=Transforming the carbon economy |url=https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/638941 |website=eurekalert.org |publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science |access-date=8 April 2024}}</ref> In 2014 Socolow became a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref name="AmAcademy">{{cite web |last1=Welles |first1=Holly |title=Faculty Honor: Socolow Elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences |url=https://environment.princeton.edu/news/faculty-honor-socolow-elected-to-the-american-academy-of-arts-and-sciences/ |website=environment.princeton.edu |publisher=Princeton University |access-date=8 April 2024}}</ref>

Socolow was a long-time member of the board of directors of the [[Audubon|National Audubon Society]].<ref name="ScottMedal" />
